name: Battle of Plassey
info: On 23 June 1757 Robert Clive's East India Company force beat the army of Nawab Siraj-ud-Daulah at Plassey in Bengal, helped by the inaction of commanders who had conspired with the Company; Mir Jafar was made Nawab.

facts.date: 23 June 1757; the fighting is said to have ended in approximately 11 hours
facts.place: Palashi (Anglicised Plassey) on the banks of the Hooghly River, about 150 kilometres (93 mi) north of Calcutta and south of Murshidabad, in West Bengal, India
facts.sides: The British East India Company under Colonel Robert Clive, with about 3,000 soldiers (some 750 European infantry, 2,100 sepoys and artillery), and a small French contingent on the other side; the Nawab Siraj-ud-Daulah, with about 50,000 soldiers including the defectors (30,000 infantry and 20,000 cavalry by the fuller count), 10 war elephants, and artillery put at anything from 40 to 300 pieces.
facts.outcome: The Nawab's army dispersed and Siraj-ud-Daulah fled; the Company occupied his camp. Clive estimated the Nawab's losses at 500 men, and British losses were estimated at 22 killed and 50 wounded, with 13 sepoys killed and 30 wounded.

t: The Company and the Nawab each had aims: the Company wanted recognition of its privileges and reparation for Calcutta, and Siraj-ud-Daulah wanted to stop the unauthorised fortifications and the loss of his revenue.
The Company's side won with a small force because of a conspiracy: Mir Jafar, Rai Durlabh and Yar Lutuf Khan brought their troops to the field but made no move, and the Nawab fled.
To deal with the merchant Omichund, Clive had two treaties drawn up, a real one on white paper and a false one on red, and Admiral Watson's signature on the false one was counterfeited.
dyk: Clive's two treaties, a real one on white paper and a false one on red to deceive Omichund, were signed by the Company's committee, but Admiral Watson signed only the real one, and his signature on the other had to be counterfeited.
ev: Alivardi Khan dies and is succeeded by his grandson Siraj-ud-Daulah, aged twenty-three
Siraj-ud-Daulah takes Calcutta, and many of the prisoners die in the Black Hole
Clive and Admiral Watson recapture Calcutta on 2 January
Clive takes the French town of Chandannagar
Mir Jafar signs the treaties with the Company on 4 June
The battle is fought on 23 June; Mir Jafar is saluted as Nawab the next day
Siraj-ud-Daulah is betrayed at Rajmahal on 2 July and murdered that night by Mir Jafar's son Miran's order
The Company defeats a Dutch force at Chinsura and replaces Mir Jafar with Mir Qasim

sections.background:
The Bengal Subah had been the largest subdivision of the Mughal Empire and later an independent state under the Nawab of Bengal. The Company held its stations at Madras, Calcutta and Bombay, and followed a policy of allying with princes and Nawabs in return for concessions. The French also had stations in India, among them Chandannagar in Bengal, and the Carnatic Wars brought British and French into proxy wars among local rulers.

Alivardi Khan had allowed the Europeans to strengthen their fortifications during the Maratha invasions, but also took large sums from them. The Company complained that it could not enjoy fully the farman of 1717, and its passes for native traders and duties on goods hurt the Nawab's revenue. Alivardi died in April 1756 and his twenty-three-year-old grandson Siraj-ud-Daulah, said to have had a ferocious temper, was suspicious of the Europeans' profits and ordered them to stop fortifying. When the British refused, he took Cossimbazar and then Calcutta, which fell on 20 June 1756, its garrison of about 500 facing a force of nearly 50,000 infantry and cavalry.

Prisoners were put into the dungeon of Fort William, the Black Hole, which held 146 and where only 23 walked out the next day. It appears that the Nawab did not know of these conditions. The Company's council at Madras sent Clive and Admiral Watson to re-establish the settlements, obtain recognition of its privileges and reparation for its losses. They retook Calcutta on 2 January 1757.
sections.forces:
Two accounts of the Nawab's strength are given. One puts his army at about 50,000, including defectors, with 40 cannon and 10 war elephants, against 3,000 under Clive. The other counts 30,000 infantry with matchlocks, swords, pikes and rockets and 20,000 cavalry, among 300 pieces of artillery, with about 50 French artillerymen under de St. Frais, and puts the Nawab's army in an arc facing the grove, 45,000 of them apart from the 5,000 cavalry and 7,000 infantry behind the French guns. Mir Jafar commanded the left, closest to the British, Yar Lutuf Khan the centre and Rai Durlabh the right.

Clive's army, after joining Major Kilpatrick, had 613 Europeans, 171 artillerymen with eight field pieces and two howitzers, 91 topasses, 2,100 sepoys and 150 sailors. In the battle account it is 750 European infantry, 100 topasses, 2,100 sepoys, 100 artillerymen and 50 sailors. Its camp was the Laksha Bagh, a mango grove 800 yards long, about a mile from the Nawab's entrenchments.

Both sides wanted something other than a plain contest. Siraj-ud-Daulah, threatened by the Afghans under Ahmad Shah Durrani and by the Marathas, could not send his entire force. The Company turned to a conspiracy with the Nawab's army chief Mir Jafar, the Jagat Seths, Yar Lutuf Khan, Omichund and Rai Durlabh, who, would bring their troops but not fight.
sections.course:
On 23 June the Nawab's army advanced from its camp towards the grove at daybreak. At 8:00 the French artillery at the larger tank fired the first shot, and the Nawab's artillery fired heavily. By 8:30 the British had lost 10 Europeans and 20 sepoys, and Clive pulled back into the shelter of the grove. After three hours nothing had changed, and the British staff decided to hold until night and attack at midnight. A heavy rainstorm then drenched the Nawab's gunpowder, which was not covered, while the British protected theirs with tarpaulins.

Believing the British guns were useless, Mir Madan Khan led a cavalry charge and was mortally wounded by grapeshot. Siraj, who had stayed in his tent, was deeply disturbed and begged Mir Jafar to defend his turban; Mir Jafar promised his service and sent word to Clive urging him on. Rai Durlabh advised Siraj to withdraw, and he left for Murshidabad on a camel with 2,000 horsemen.

At about 14:00 the Nawab's army turned back to its entrenchments. Major Kilpatrick advanced on the French position, and Clive, reprimanding him for acting without orders, led the army to take it at 15:00. Clive checked a division that turned out to be Mir Jafar's, then took the redoubt and the hill beyond it. The British held the entrenchment and the abandoned camp by 17:00.
sections.aftermath:
On the evening of 23 June Mir Jafar wrote to Clive, and on the next morning at Daudpur Clive embraced him and saluted him as Nawab of Bengal, Bihar and Odisha. Mir Jafar reached Murshidabad on 24 June, and Clive arrived on 29 June with 200 European soldiers and 300 sepoys, in the wake of rumours of an attempt on his life, and placed Mir Jafar on the throne.

Siraj-ud-Daulah reached Murshidabad at midnight on 23 June and escaped northwards by boat with his wife and jewels on the night of 24 June. He was discovered on 2 July at Rajmahal, betrayed to the local military governor, who was Mir Jafar's brother, and handed over to Mir Jafar's son Miran, who had him murdered that night. His remains were paraded through Murshidabad and buried at the tomb of Alivardi Khan.

The treaty gave the British all the land within the Maratha Ditch and 600 yards beyond it, and the zamindari of land between Calcutta and the sea, and required 22,000,000 rupees (£2,750,000) in restitution. Siraj's wealth proved far less than expected, so a council on 29 June decided that half would be paid at once. When it was revealed to Omichund that he would receive nothing, he is said to have gone insane. Clive reported 22 British killed and 50 wounded, and estimated that the Nawab lost 500 men.
sections.sources:
The battle is known largely from British works: Robert Orme's History of the Military Transactions (1861 edition), Malleson's Decisive Battles of India (1885), S. C. Hill's Bengal in 1756-1757 (1905), the Memoirs of the Revolution in Bengal (1760) by John Campbell and William Watts, and Peter Harrington's Plassey 1757 (1994). Clive's testimony to the House of Commons on 10 May 1773 is his own defence of the conspiracy: he called Omichund a great villain whom it was true policy and justice to deceive.

The figures differ. The Nawab's army appears as about 50,000, including defectors, with 40 cannon, and as 30,000 infantry and 20,000 cavalry with 300 pieces of artillery; Clive's force as 3,000, and in detail as 613 Europeans, 2,100 sepoys and others. The battle is said to have lasted approximately 11 hours, though the sequence given runs from 8:00 to about 17:00. The 500 lost by the Nawab is Clive's own estimate, and a name in his testimony, Duprée, may be a mistranscription of Dupleix.

The money is reported with attributions: the historian W. Dalrymple gives the Jagat Seths' offer to Clive and the Company of more than £4m and 110,000 rupees a month for Company troops, and Omichund's demand is given as three million rupees. The battle is called decisive, yet the result is put down to Mir Jafar's betrayal, the Nawab's flight and the commitment of much of the Bengal army against the Afghan invasion.
sections.legacy:
Plassey was a step towards colonial control of the Indian subcontinent. The British gained wealth and influence over Mir Jafar, extracted concessions for earlier losses and trade income, and used the revenue to build military strength and push out other European powers. The French were no longer a significant force in Bengal. The battle helped the Company take complete control of Bengal in 1773.

The settlement was unstable. By 1759 Mir Jafar, finding his position as a subordinate to the British intolerable, encouraged the Dutch to advance against them. The Dutch sent seven large ships and 1,400 men from Java, and Clive defeated them at Chinsura on 25 November 1759. The British then deposed Mir Jafar and installed Mir Qasim. Clive returned to England, was made Baron Clive of Plassey in the Irish peerage and obtained a seat in the House of Commons.

The struggle continued in the south, where Eyre Coote defeated a French garrison in 1761, and the French, returned Pondicherry in 1763, never regained their former stature. The British would emerge as rulers of the subcontinent in subsequent years. A monument, the Palashi Monument, stands on the battlefield.

summary: At Plassey on 23 June 1757 a small East India Company force under Robert Clive defeated the army of Nawab Siraj-ud-Daulah, whose commander Mir Jafar and other officers had conspired with the Company and did not fight. Mir Jafar became Nawab, and Siraj-ud-Daulah was killed.
references: Sushil Chaudhary, The Prelude to Empire: Plassey Revolution of 1757 (Manohar, 2000)
P.J. Marshall, Bengal – the British Bridgehead (Cambridge University Press, 1987)
Thomas G.P. Spear, Master of Bengal – Clive and His India (Thames and Hudson, 1975)
notes: Strengths conflict inside the article: 50,000 / 40 cannon / 10 elephants vs 3,000 in the lead; 30,000 infantry, 20,000 cavalry, 300 guns in the battle account; British 613 Europeans etc. (approach march) vs 750 Europeans etc. (battle). Both given with their places.
The article says 'approximately 11 hours' for the battle, but its battle account runs from 8:00 to about 17:00 (nine hours); not reconciled.
'45,000 formed an arc' is in addition to the 12,000 behind the French; I did not add them up, only told them.

Bribes: the Dalrymple figure (£4m, 110,000 rupees a month) is the only attributed sum; Omichund's demand is 30 lakhs, the article also says 'three million rupees (£300,000)'. The article does not give the sums paid to Mir Jafar's side other than the 22,000,000 rupees restitution. I did not give the Nandkumar bribe at Hooghly (the article says he was bribed to stay inactive at Chandannagar) for space.

The 'Sources' section lists works from the article's References and Further reading; the article gives no discussion of which accounts are reliable, so the section on what historians dispute is limited to the figures and the cause of the result. This is thin.
In the legacy I give 'complete control of Bengal in 1773' as the article does; the article's lead and later text do not explain the date.
The article gives the Black Hole figures (146 / 23) as fact; no historians' dispute about them appears in it. Told as given.

Not found: any Mughal view, Siraj's own aims in his words, the battle's name for the Nawab's army (Bengali sources), the numbers of French. The sentence 'Clive's quotation has a note that a name in it may be a mistranscription' is mine, from the article's bracketed note.
